newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish growth raises fears on inflation and debt.
newsitem.headline: Turkish growth raises fears on inflation and debt.

text.p: Turkey's economy grew by nearly eight percent in real terms last year, raising fears the economy is overheating.
Markets reacted calmly to the news on Monday but analysts warned Turkey faces increasing inflation, ballooning government debt and a burgeoning trade deficit.

Analysts said there are few signs that the government, which starts talks with a delegation from the International Monetary Fund on Tuesday, was prepared to take action to slow growth and reduce inflation.

"The expected slow-down in the first quarter of 1997 does not look to be there," said economist Turgut Tokgoz. "And the economy does not look like it is going to cool down on its own, so it looks like Turkey is going to experience further growth at the expense of upset macroeconomic and fiscal balances."
On Monday the state statistics institute reported real gross national product rose by 7.9 percent in 1996 compared with 8.0 percent in 1995.
The economy grew at an annual rate of 8.8 percent in fourth quarter 1996, faster than the 8.0 percent in fourth quarter 1995.
"Turkey has been growing by 8.0 percent for two years, but it has external deficits -- the economy needs to be slowed down," economics professor and columnist Deniz Gokce told Reuters.
Analysts expect Turkey's foreign trade deficit to be around $20 billion for 1996, up from $14.1 billion in 1995.
Inflation is currently running at around 78 percent a year and the government budget deficit was $10.6 billion, or 8.2 percent of gross national product, in 1996.
The figures did not affect the financial markets, which were expecting a rise of between 7.5 and eight percent for gross national product, brokers said.
The stock market rose by 3.93 percent on Monday.
But analysts, focusing on the long term, were more worried.
"At this stage I don't think the figures are inflationary. Turkey has high inflation anyway and I don't think this will make it any higher," an analyst at a private bank told Reuters.
"But if this figure is even five or six percent in 1997 it will be too high. If it reaches 14 percent as predicted by (Premier Necmettin) Erbakan, that will be a crisis environment."
The State Planning Organisation has set its 1997 growth target at four percent.
Bankers said they hoped Erbakan's government would negotiate a stand-by credit from the IMF to help the economy. But the government was showing few signs it intended to control growth.

Gokce said a series of high pay rises to public workers and the government's incessant need to borrow to cover losses from uncollected tax and from the outdated social security system would ensure inflation remained high and debts large.
He added that the government could not simply raise interest rates to combat inflation, as Western countries do.
"The problem in Turkey is so extensive, the budget deficit is so big, that the factors which normally control the economy completely derail things," Gokce said.

Bankers say that Turkish interest rates are so high already that they actually fuel inflation. The government's domestic debt was 3,149 trillion lira ($29 billion) at the end of 1996 -- up 131 percent from a year ago -- fuelling a need to continue borrowing and making the government vulnerable to market pressures.
